When born, animals and humans are thrown into an unknown world forced to use their sensory inputs for survival. As they begin to understand and develop their senses they are able to navigate and interact with their environment. The process in which we learn to do this is called reinforcement learning. This is the idea that learning comes from a series of trial and error where there exists rewards and punishments for every action. The brain naturally logs these events as experiences, and decides new actions based on past experience. An action resulting in a reward will then be higher favored than an action resulting in a punishment. Using this concept, autonomous systems, such as robots, can learn about their environment in the same way. Using simulated sensory data from ultrasonic sensors, moisture sensors, encoders, shock sensors, pressure sensors, and steepness sensors, a robotic system will be able to make decisions on how to navigate through its environment to reach a goal. The robotic system will not know the source of the data or the terrain it is navigating. Given a map of an open environment simulating an area after a natural disaster, the robot will use model-free temporal difference learning with exploration to find the best path to a goal in terms of distance, safety, and terrain navigation. Two forms of temporal difference learning will be tested; off-policy (Q-Learning) and onpolicy (Sarsa). Through experimentation with several world map sizes, it is found that the off-policy algorithm, Q-Learning, is the most reliable and efficient in terms of navigating a known map with unequal states.

This is essentially a "rough draft" of an ongoing project to sonify local air quality data. This project uses the purpleair.com air monitor network to create chords from four air monitors of a user's choice and output those chords via midi (for use in a DAW or directly). Essentially, this highlights difference in air quality between monitors - for instance, to highlight differences in air quality between different neighborhoods in a city. If there is little difference in air quality, only one or two notes will be played, while large differences in air quality will lead to large chords over several octaves. This code was used for a live performance by Diegetic at The Embassy on March 7th, 2020.

Program to detect keypoints in an image according to the following steps, which are also the first three steps of Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT). 1. Generate four octaves. Each octave is composed of five images blurred using Gaussian kernels. For each octave, the bandwidth parameters σ (five different scales) of the Gaussian kernels are shown in Tab. 1. 2. Compute Difference of Gaussian (DoG) for all four octaves. 3. Detect key points which are located at the maxima or minima of the DoG images.

Tellus Heightmap Generator is program that generates random heightmaps based on given variables and allows users to export them either as a Targa texture or as an OBJ mesh file. The randomness of the heightmap is done through 2D Perlin noise using the number of octaves and the amount of persistence the user inputs. The user can also change the level of detail, or LOD, of the mesh as well as the difference in height between the highest and lowest points. Tellus was written in C++ and GLSL and was completed over a 2.5 month period.

A ‘pitch’ may have both musical and linguistic references. As far as music is concerned, ‘absolute ear’ is a commonly ringing phenomenon. In case of the latter, experts who specialize in perfecting linguistic tones to understand language variations will find it an extremely common tool. While many consider relative pitch to be far more important, absolute pitch training has an equal footing in understanding both music and language in general. Postmodernists may not adhere to absolutism but they cannot deny the necessity of the training environment that an absolute ear provides. It serves as a reference to near-perfection for the individual to be able to imitate a determined pitch.   How does absolute pitch training truly benefit? When one can conveniently train in relative pitch, why is there any requirement to train in absolute ear? Relative pitch is more about reconstructing a given tune or composition. Here, a reference note is required in order to position the relative pitch appropriately. If for instance, a singer finds the pre-determined pitch too high or low, they can scale up or scale down to a more convenient pitch. To understand how this is done, the musician should be able to do three things:  Chalk out an appropriate difference between the apparent note and the reference note  Fix proper intervals between the given tones  The ability to pitch a note in the melody of a composition. This is especially expected of singers and the accuracy of the distance between two notes has to be very high.  Already established singers with both relative pitch and absolute pitch training will be able to use their musical abilities to their best. With the right method of training, a seasoned singer will find it easier to transfer their melodic talents to particular instruments. Pitch perfection can be applied to fretless, string instruments such as violin or viola.   Some experts promise better results with relative pitch perfection. Recreating melodies forms the very basis of music, which greatly validates this method of vocal and instrumental training. It is however not true that perfect pitch recognition is futile. For a better understanding of what it is about, you must look at perfect pitch as a landmark that directs you towards the right path. In music, this is your ‘absolute’ or ‘perfect’ point of departure. This phenomenon is greatly applicable to a Capella music, which has practically no reference note, where the essence of the music lies in the singers themselves who create or recreate them.  A guided learning experience must include both listening and speaking. Most experts will tell you that adept listening is the key to mastering the perfect ear. Developing an ear for the right note requires a lot of patience, as it develops only with ceaseless practice. While hiring a teacher is the conventionally accepted method, another better alternative is to go for software training. This allows you access to the pitch correction modules and applications whenever required. Also, this is a one-time investment, unlike tutorials that charge you on a monthly or per sitting basis.  Trying to understand the difference between relativism and absolutism in music and language can be difficult at first. In fact, those who have an absolute ear may not be able to adapt to recognizing changing patterns within different fields of music. Those who experience rigidity in acknowledging relative differences may actually be wrongfully deemed ‘absolute purists who cannot stand tonal varieties.’ The truth lies in the difference between people who can perceive within the 440 Hz range and those beyond that. Also, linguistic and cultural differences apply to both language and music and may pose limitations in understanding how absolutism and relativism applies to both. A question of impending bias towards one’s own culture also comes into the picture, for a person no matter how liberal he is, can never be out of influence of a particular culture.   While absolute ear training can be very useful in certain spheres of music and language, they can also be limiting to the person who is more or less accustomed to only 440 Hz tonal frequency. Imagine if every song were to be played or sung within the aural range, there would be nothing but uniformity! It is important to perceive relativism in conjunction with absolutism for only a balanced outlook will help in a thorough understanding of musical art and communication.   listening-ear-trainer provides online software for relative pitch and absolute pitch training. The absolute pitch training methodology is easily accessible once it has been subscribed for. It includes dozens of exercises for mastering The Singing Funnel Method and The Octave Anchor Pitches Method.
